chunks: How an ADC works. The question: How does an ADC work?
An ADC (analog-to-digital converter) turns a voltage into a number that a microcontroller can use. It does this in three steps.
It samples, meaning it grabs the voltage at one instant. It quantizes, meaning it decides which of a fixed set of equal steps the voltage falls in.
Then it outputs that step's number as a binary code.
Imagine a ruler with 4,096 tick marks spread over 3. 3 volts. You hold a voltage up to the ruler and report the nearest tick below it.
You can never report a value between two ticks, so there is always a small rounding error.
If the voltage wiggles while you read it, your reading blurs, so the ADC freezes the voltage first and measures the frozen copy.
The conversion chain. Two inputs control it: the sample clock decides when the voltage is measured, and the reference decides what a code is worth .
Everything to the left of the quantizer is analog and sets noise and aliasing; everything to the right is digital and exact.
Resolution (bits): how many binary digits the code has. N bits gives 2 to the N possible steps. Reference voltage: the voltage that marks the top of the ruler.
The ADC measures the input as a fraction of it. LSB: the size of one step, the reference divided by 2 to the N .
Quantization error: the rounding error from snapping to a step: up to one step if you report the tick below, half a step if you report the middle of the step.
Sample-and-hold: ("What is sample and hold?") : the circuit that freezes the voltage while it is measured.
Take a 12-bit ADC with a 3. 3 volts reference. It has 2 to the 12 equals 4096 steps, so each step is 3. 3 / 4096, about 0. 8 millivolts. An input of 1.
65 volts is exactly half of the reference, so the code is 2048, half of 4096. A 1. 6504 volts input would give the same code, because it is less than one step higher.
That is the whole idea.
"An ADC samples the input, holds it steady, then compares it to a reference to pick one of 2 to the N levels and outputs that level as a binary code.
Resolution is the reference divided by 2 to the N , so a 12-bit ADC on 3. 3 volts has about 0. 8 millivolts per step.

How it finds the level depends on architecture: flash uses one comparator per level for speed, SAR does a binary search in N steps and is what most microcontrollers use, and delta-sigma oversamples to get very high resolution at low speed.
I'd always add an anti-alias filter and a clean reference."
